title: MCP = Mega Context Problem - Matt Carey

summary: Matt Carey, who works on MCP and agents at Cloudflare, explores the challenge of making every API accessible to AI agents. The talk traces the evolution from bundled tools—where each developer recreated tools for services like Gmail—through the MCP explosion where service providers offered standardized MCP tools as another API surface alongside CLIs and REST. The core problem emerged when attempting full API coverage: Cloudflare's OpenAPI spec is 2.3 million tokens, and converting all endpoints to tools produces roughly 1.1 million tokens, overwhelming any agent's context window. Cloudflare's initial workaround of splitting the API into 16 product-based MCP servers provided incomplete coverage and forced users to manually select servers. Carey argues MCP itself isn't the problem; dumping all tools into context is. He presents three progressive discovery approaches. CLI-based interaction lets agents invoke commands like Wrangler and use --help for introspection, but requires shell access. Tool search performs keyword matching to load only relevant tools, though it still loads unused definitions. Code mode lets agents write TypeScript code against typed SDKs generated from OpenAPI specs, leveraging types as concise input/output descriptions. Cloudflare demonstrated code mode listing and deploying workers, including adding Access protection. The major barrier was security: executing untrusted LLM-generated code risks secret exposure, data exfiltration, infinite loops, and resource consumption. Carey demonstrates Cloudflare Workers (V8 isolates) as a primitive for safely executing code from strings, showing that process.env contains no secrets, network access can be programmatically controlled via booleans or custom functions, and the sandbox runs on the backend rather than the browser. He notes similar primitives emerging from Pydantic Monty, Deno, and WorkerD. Carey envisions a future where code becomes a compact plan—replacing many tool calls with one 'code' tool—and where APIs must be hardened for AI-driven traffic with proper rate limiting. On the client side, he predicts programmatic tool calling, saved mini-scripts that agents generate and maintain (e.g., for cron jobs or web scraping), and a proliferation of MCP clients as the SDK becomes lightweight enough to embed natively in frameworks. He expects MCP to become middleware—simply a flag like 'MCP = true' in frameworks like Next.js—exposing all APIs over MCP by default. The TypeScript SDK is being refined to fit in any bundle, with native integration in major frameworks expected by end of year.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Agent Humor
sections.summary: Matt Carey introduces himself, works on MCP and agents at Cloudflare. Jokes about agent behavior fluctuation and introduces the core question: how do we give agents hands to interact with the outside world?

sections.title: Evolution of Tool Calling
sections.summary: Traces the history from bundled tools (each developer recreating tools for services like Gmail) through shared tools to the MCP explosion where service providers offer standardized MCP tools as another API surface alongside CLIs and REST/GraphQL.

sections.title: The Context Window Problem
sections.summary: Explains that naively converting all API endpoints to MCP tools explodes the context window. Cloudflare's OpenAPI spec is 2.3 million tokens, producing ~1.1 million tokens of tool definitions, which won't fit even in the largest foundation models.

sections.title: Splitting APIs into Product-Based MCP Servers
sections.summary: Describes Cloudflare's initial workaround: 16 product-based MCP servers covering ~2,600 endpoints. This reduced context but forced users to select servers manually and provided incomplete coverage (e.g., 6 tools vs 30 endpoints per product).

sections.title: Progressive Discovery and MCP's Role
sections.summary: Introduces progressive discovery as the solution. Argues MCP is not dead—it's a protocol. The problem is dumping all tools into context at once. Three approaches are previewed: CLI, tool search, and a third option (code mode).

sections.title: CLI-Based Agent Interaction
sections.summary: Demonstrates how agents can use CLIs like Wrangler, reading command outputs and using --help for introspection. Popular with tools like OpenClaude but limited by the requirement for shell access.

sections.title: Tool Search Approach
sections.summary: Describes Claude Code's tool search: keyword matching on user questions loads relevant tools into context. Works well but loads unused definitions—example shows 2,100 tokens loaded with only 500 used.

sections.title: Code Mode: Agents Writing TypeScript
sections.summary: Introduces code mode: generating TypeScript types from OpenAPI specs and letting agents write code against a typed SDK. Demonstrates listing workers, deploying a 'Hello world' worker, and adding Cloudflare Access protection—all via agent-generated code.

sections.title: Security Concerns and V8 Isolates
sections.summary: Explains why clients didn't adopt code mode: running untrusted LLM-generated code is inherently risky (secret access, exfiltration, infinite loops, resource consumption). Positions Cloudflare Workers (V8 isolates) as a primitive for safely executing code from strings.

sections.title: Demonstrating the V8 Isolate Sandbox
sections.summary: Demonstrates that code runs on the backend in a fully isolated dynamic worker, not the browser. Shows process.env contains no secrets, a Cloudflare global exists, and turning off Node compatibility removes process.env entirely. The sandbox is programmable with configurable guardrails.

sections.title: Programmable Network Guardrails
sections.summary: Shows that workers can be blocked from accessing the internet by default, with network access toggleable via a boolean. More granular control is possible via custom functions limiting access to specific domains, as used on Cloudflare's MCP.

sections.title: Cloudflare MCP Client Demo
sections.summary: Demonstrates an MCP client with auth screen pop-up, providing read-only access to the entire Cloudflare API (~2,000+ endpoints). Can list workers, deploy, add access protection, inspect DNS, send emails, and more.

sections.title: Future of Agent Tool Access
sections.summary: Surveys the landscape of agent tool access: CLIs on local machines or VMs, isolated untrusted code execution, tool search, UI rendering. Predicts many isolated environments on the web and infrastructure primitives for running untrusted code, since code is a compact plan with more degrees of freedom than individual tool calls.

sections.title: Emerging Untrusted Code Primitives
sections.summary: Shows examples of untrusted code execution primitives: WorkerD spawning dynamic workers, Deno run, and Pydantic Monty's Python code interpreter. Notes that running untrusted code used to be unthinkable (a CVE), but LLMs are good at writing code to run.

sections.title: Historical Perspective and API Readiness
sections.summary: Draws parallel to 1950s punch cards as early untrusted code execution, notes the cloud moved away from this, and predicts a return as AI users write code against services. Warns that APIs must be hardened with rate limiting because agents can hammer APIs from multiple sandboxes simultaneously.

sections.title: Client-Side Innovation
sections.summary: Predicts programmatic tool calling in clients, saved mini-scripts that users keep for later reuse (e.g., cron jobs, web scraping), and many more MCP clients as the SDK simplifies. Notes building MCP clients was hard due to stateful connections and resumability, leading to stalled innovation. Envisions stateless agent loops as agents scale to 100 per person.

sections.title: MCP as Middleware and SDK Future
sections.summary: Predicts MCP will become middleware—a flag like 'MCP = true' in frameworks. The TypeScript SDK is becoming lightweight enough to fit in any bundle, with native integration expected in major TypeScript full-stack frameworks by end of year, exposing all APIs over MCP. References the Code Mode blog post about giving agents an entire API in a thousand tokens.
